# Metrics & Time-Series Systems (Prometheus / Datadog)

## Problem

Design target (hypothetical, for sizing practice): 1B samples/sec. 30-day retention. Query: "CPU > 90% for 5+ min". <100ms query latency.

All sizes and rates below are assumptions used to do the arithmetic, not measurements.

## Architecture

```
 ┌─────┐   pull    ┌───────────┐  write  ┌──────┐
 │ App │◄──────────│ Collector │────────►│ TSDB │
 └─────┘  (15s)    └───────────┘         └──┬───┘
                                            │
                                      ┌─────▼─────┐
                                      │  Query +  │
                                      │  alerting │
                                      └───────────┘
```

```
Sample (one data point):
  ├─ timestamp: 1609459200000
  ├─ name: "http_request_latency"
  ├─ labels: {method, endpoint, status}
  └─ value: 45.3 (ms)

Collector (Prometheus-style, pull model):
  ├─ Scrape endpoints every 15 sec
  ├─ Parse, buffer ~1 min in memory
  └─ Write to the time-series database

Time-series database (TSDB):
  ├─ Target ingest: 1B samples/sec (design target)
  ├─ Compress values, delta-encode timestamps
  ├─ Partition by day or hour (fast pruning)
  └─ Retention: 30 days

Query engine:
  ├─ PromQL: avg_over_time(cpu_usage[1h])
  ├─ Aggregation: sum, avg, max, quantile
  └─ Alerts: fire when a condition holds
```

No single node ingests 1B/sec: collectors and TSDB shards scale out horizontally (see sharding below).

## Time-Series Compression

```
Raw sample (uncompressed, assumed sizes):
  ├─ Timestamp: 8 bytes
  ├─ Value: 8 bytes (float64)
  ├─ Labels: ~200 bytes (assumed)
  └─ Total: ~216 bytes

1B samples/sec * 216 B = 216 GB/sec uncompressed

1. Delta-of-delta (timestamps):
   ├─ Sample 1: store the raw timestamp, 1000
   ├─ Sample 2: ts 1015, delta = 15
   ├─ Sample 3: ts 1030, delta = 15,
   │            delta-of-delta = 0
   └─ Regular scrapes give delta-of-delta = 0,
      which packs into about one bit

2. XOR for floats (Gorilla-style):
   ├─ XOR each value with the previous one
   ├─ Similar readings leave long runs of zero bits
   └─ Store only the meaningful middle bits

3. Label pooling:
   ├─ ~1000 unique label sets (assumed): store once
   ├─ Samples reference a series ID
   └─ Sample = [series_id, ts, value], not labels
```

```
Planning budget (assumption, not a measurement):
  ├─ Assume ~15 bytes/sample after compression
  │  (conservative; measure real bytes/sample)
  └─ 1B/sec * 15 B = 15 GB/sec

Storage per day at that budget:
  ├─ 1B/sec * 86,400 sec = 86.4B samples/day
  ├─ At 15 bytes/sample: ~1.3 TB/day
  └─ 30 days: ~39 TB
```

## Partitioning & Retention

```
Partition by time (one file per day):

  day_0.db   ~1.3 TB   oldest, dropped first
  day_1.db   ~1.3 TB
  ...
  day_29.db  ~1.3 TB
  day_30.db  ~1.3 TB   today, being written

Benefits:
  ├─ "Last 7 days": read 7 files (~9 TB, not ~39 TB)
  ├─ Expire data: drop a whole file, no compaction
  └─ Parallelism: read different days in parallel
```

```
Shard by series, not by metric name:

  shard = hash(name + labels) % K

  Parallel ingestion: collectors → K shards
  Spreads one very busy metric across all shards.

  Sharding by metric name instead would put a hot
  metric on one node and overload it.
```

## Query Examples

```
# Mean over the last hour, per series
avg_over_time(
  http_request_latency{endpoint="/api/users"}[1h])

# P99 from a histogram (uses the _bucket series)
histogram_quantile(0.99,
  sum by (le) (rate(http_request_latency_bucket[5m])))

# Requests per second
rate(http_requests_total[1m])
```

```yaml
# Alerting rule (Prometheus 2.x rule file)
- alert: HighCPU
  expr: avg(cpu_usage) > 90
  for: 5m
```

```
Query cost:
  ├─ Parse: negligible
  ├─ Find series: inverted index on labels
  │  (postings lists), not a B-tree
  ├─ Read chunks that overlap the time range
  └─ Aggregate: O(samples touched)
```

## Cardinality Explosion

```
Problem: unbounded labels cause series explosion

Bad: http_request_latency{method, endpoint, user_id}

  Unique series = product of label values:
    ├─ 10 methods
    ├─ 1000 endpoints
    ├─ 1M users
    └─ = 10B series

  Every active series costs index and memory,
  so 10B series cannot fit. Cost scales with
  series count, not just sample rate.

Good: http_request_latency{method, endpoint, status}
    ├─ 10 methods
    ├─ 1000 endpoints
    ├─ 10 statuses
    └─ = 100K series (manageable)

  user_id is NOT a label (unbounded)
  → record it in logs or traces instead

Rule of thumb:
  ├─ Cardinality = product of unique label values
  ├─ Set a series budget per metric
  └─ Watch active-series count and scrape time;
     a sudden jump means a label exploded
```

## Failure Modes

```
Collector crashes:
  ├─ App keeps serving /metrics (pull model:
  │  the app buffers nothing for it)
  ├─ Recovery: restart collector, scraping resumes
  └─ Data loss: the gap while it was down

TSDB full:
  ├─ Ingest rate exceeded the plan
  ├─ Solution: shorten retention or add capacity
  └─ Alert on disk usage well before it fills

Cardinality explosion:
  ├─ A new label is added (e.g. user_id)
  ├─ Series multiply: 100K → 100B
  ├─ TSDB runs out of memory
  └─ Prevention: review label changes, enforce limits
```

---

## Interview Checklist

- [ ] Delta-of-delta compression for timestamps
- [ ] XOR compression for floats
- [ ] Partitioning by time for retention
- [ ] Cardinality control (label limits)
- [ ] Scale (assumed target): 1B samples/sec, 30-day retention, ~39 TB at the assumed 15 bytes/sample
- [ ] Query: PromQL, aggregations, alerting
- [ ] Indexes: efficient time-range queries

## Common Wrong Answers

- ❌ "Store raw metrics" — at the assumed 216 bytes/sample that is ~18.7 PB/day, unsustainable
- ❌ "Add all labels" — cardinality explosion
- ❌ "Keep all data forever" — storage grows unbounded
- ❌ "No compression" — delta-of-delta and XOR encoding are what make the budget work
